claim: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) encodes seasonal changes in the environment.
source: Annual changes in the environment threaten survival, and numerous biological processes in mammals adjust to this challenge via seasonal encoding by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: When days are short, SCN neurons display unified rhythms with synchronous phasing.
source: To tune behavior according to day length, SCN neurons display unified rhythms with synchronous phasing when days are short, but will divide into two sub-clusters when days are long.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the photoperiodic states of the SCN.

claim: When days are long, SCN neurons divide into two sub-clusters.
source: To tune behavior according to day length, SCN neurons display unified rhythms with synchronous phasing when days are short, but will divide into two sub-clusters when days are long.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the photoperiodic states of the SCN.

claim: A switch in chloride transport and GABAA signaling is critical for maintaining state plasticity in the SCN network.
source: Here we identify that a switch in chloride transport and GABAA signaling is critical for maintaining state plasticity in the SCN network.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Blocking excitatory GABAA signaling locks the SCN into its long day state.
source: Further, we reveal that blocking excitatory GABAA signaling locks the SCN into its long day state.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by acetazolamide experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The SCN is a master pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus.
source: In mammals, the circadian system is a hierarchical collection of biological clocks orchestrated by a master pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the anterior hypothalamus (Mohawk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: SCN neurons display ca. 24 hr rhythms in electrical and molecular activity.
source: At the cellular level, SCN neurons display ca. 24 hr rhythms in electrical and molecular activity (Hastings et al., 2018) generated by genetic feedback loops that control daily expression of clock proteins (Buhr and Takahashi, 2013) and the clock-controlled genes that regulate cellular physiology (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Intercellular interactions among SCN neurons synchronize, amplify, and stabilize rhythms of cells within the network.
source: Although the circadian molecular clock drives cellular rhythms, intercellular interactions among SCN neurons synchronize, amplify, and stabilize rhythms of cells within the network (Evans, 2016; Hastings et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Seasonal encoding is accomplished via changes in the spatiotemporal relationships of SCN clock cells.
source: Although daily timekeeping is a cellular property, seasonal encoding is accomplished via changes in the spatiotemporal relationships of SCN clock cells (Meijer et al., 2010; Evans and Gorman, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: When days are long, the SCN network switches to an alternate state characterized by two subclusters of clock neurons that cycle in anti-phase.
source: In contrast, when days are long, the SCN network switches to an alternate state characterized by two subclusters of clock neurons that cycle in anti-phase (Evans et al., 2013; Inagaki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Seasonal affective disorder affects 3–10% of people.
source: In humans, seasonality likewise influences a wide range of functions such as sleep, metabolism, and neurotransmission (Garbazza and Benedetti, 2018), which can produce annually recurrent pathology in 3–10% of people (Wehr et al., 2001; Lewy et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: GABA is the primary neurotransmitter expressed by SCN neurons.
source: GABA is the primary neurotransmitter expressed by SCN neurons (Albers et al., 2017), and recent work indicates that day length modulates GABA signaling in the SCN network (Evans et al., 2013; Myung et al., 2015; Farajnia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Day length modulates GABA signaling in the SCN network.
source: GABA is the primary neurotransmitter expressed by SCN neurons (Albers et al., 2017), and recent work indicates that day length modulates GABA signaling in the SCN network (Evans et al., 2013; Myung et al., 2015; Farajnia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The GABAA receptor can elicit either hyperpolarization or depolarization depending on the electrochemical gradient of chloride.
source: Although GABA is typically classified as an inhibitory neurotransmitter, the GABAA receptor is a heteropentameric ligand-gated ion channel permeable to chloride and bicarbonate that can elicit either hyperpolarization or depolarization depending on the electrochemical gradient of chloride (Kaila et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: In mature neurons, levels of intracellular chloride are regulated by KCC2 and NKCC1.
source: In mature neurons, levels of intracellular chloride are regulated by the Cl- extruder KCC2 (K+ Cl- co-transporter 2) and the Cl- importer NKCC1 (Na+ K+ Cl- co-transporter 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Exposure to long days increases the number of neurons that respond to GABA with depolarization.
source: In the SCN, recent work has shown that exposure to long days increases the number of neurons that respond to GABA with depolarization (Farajnia et al., 2014) and elevates intracellular chloride (Myung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Long days elevate intracellular chloride in SCN neurons.
source: In the SCN, recent work has shown that exposure to long days increases the number of neurons that respond to GABA with depolarization (Farajnia et al., 2014) and elevates intracellular chloride (Myung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Long days alter the waveform of the GABA-induced resetting rhythm in the SCN.
source: In L20 slices, GABA elicited phase delays for a larger proportion of the circadian cycle and produced phase advances at later times relative to L12 slices (Figure 1A–C). These results indicate that the waveform of the GABA-induced resetting rhythm is altered by photoperiod, as illustrated by either a phase response curve (Figure 1A) or polar plot (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Long day exposure does not alter systematically the magnitude of resetting to GABA.
source: On the other hand, long day exposure did not alter systematically the magnitude of resetting to this dose of GABA (Figure 1C) or vehicle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which distinguishes it from photoperiodic suppression of NMDA- (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and light-induced resetting (Pittendrigh et al., 1984; vanderLeest et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GABA-induced resetting is mediated by GABAA signaling and not GABAB signaling.
source: Importantly, this resetting response was blocked by the GABAA receptor antagonist bicuculline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with a prior study demonstrating that GABA-induced resetting is mediated by GABAA signaling and not GABAB signaling (Liu and Reppert, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: Long days increase mRNA encoding NKCC1 relative to KCC2 in the SCN.
source: Long days increase mRNA encoding NKCC1 relative to KCC2 in the SCN (Myung et al., 2015), but the switch to excitatory GABAA signaling in other neural circuits of the adult brain is often driven by post-translational downregulation of KCC2 (Chung, 2012; Hewitt et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2011; Ostroumov et al., 2016; Sarkar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Under L12, KCC2/NKCC1 fluctuated over the day in the SCN core.
source: Under L12, KCC2/NKCC1 fluctuated over the day (Figure 2B–C) in the specific SCN compartment receiving dense retinal innervation (Abrahamson and Moore, 2001). Specifically, KCC2/NKCC1 varied in the SCN core (Figure 2C, Circwave cosinor rhythmicity test: p<0.05), but not in the SCN shell (Figure 2C, Circwave cosinor rhythmicity test: p>0.5) due to region-specific expression of both chloride co-transporters (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: KCC2 expression was 91-fold lower in the AVP+ shell versus the non-AVP-expressing core.
source: In the SCN, KCC2 expression was 91-fold lower in the AVP+ shell versus the non-AVP-expressing core (Student's t: p<0.005), but KCC2 levels did not vary over the day in either region (Figure 2D, Circwave cosinor rhythmicity test: p>0.2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: L20 eliminated the daily rhythm of KCC2/NKCC1 in the SCN core.
source: Notably, L20 eliminated the daily rhythm of KCC2/NKCC1 in the SCN core (Figure 2B–C, Circwave cosinor rhythmicity test: p>0.4) by decreasing the mean daily expression of KCC2 (Figure 2D–E, LSM contrasts: p<0.01).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: L20 decreased the mean daily expression of KCC2 in the SCN core.
source: Notably, L20 eliminated the daily rhythm of KCC2/NKCC1 in the SCN core (Figure 2B–C, Circwave cosinor rhythmicity test: p>0.4) by decreasing the mean daily expression of KCC2 (Figure 2D–E, LSM contrasts: p<0.01).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: L20 increased NKCC1 expression in the SCN shell.
source: In the SCN shell, L20 increased NKCC1 expression (Figure 2F, LSM contrasts: p<0.01) and disrupted the daily rhythm of NKCC1 (Circwave cosinor rhythmicity test: p>0.1) due to elevation at specific times of the light:dark cycle (Figure 2D, LSM contrasts: p<0.01).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and 2F.

claim: Both BU and VU increased SCN period by 0.35 hr in L12 slices.
source: In L12 slices, we found that both BU and VU increased SCN period by 0.35 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which was blocked by co-culture with the GABAA receptor antagonists bicuculline or gabazine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibition of KCC2 and NKCC1 modulates the function of the SCN molecular clock by altering GABAA signaling.
source: Importantly, these results indicate that inhibition of KCC2 and NKCC1 modulates the function of the SCN molecular clock by altering GABAA signaling, which is consistent with previous work demonstrating these compounds alter chloride transport, neuronal excitability, and GABA-evoked calcium responses (Farajnia et al., 2014; Haam et al., 2012; Deisz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data with citations to support the mechanism.

claim: In vivo exposure to L20 reorganized the SCN by imposing a large phase difference between the SCN shell and core on the first cycle in vitro.
source: Consistent with previous work (Evans et al., 2013), in vivo exposure to L20 reorganized the SCN by imposing a large phase difference between the SCN shell and core on the first cycle in vitro (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and citation to prior work.

claim: The SCN network recovers from its reorganized state in vitro largely due to intercellular signals that modulate the phase and period of SCN core neurons.
source: Overall, these results indicate that the SCN network recovers from its reorganized state in vitro largely due to intercellular signals that modulate the phase and period of SCN core neurons (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: VU accelerated the process of network resynchronization in the negative direction in L20 SCN slices.
source: When L20 SCN slices were cultured with the KCC2 inhibitor VU, the process of network resynchronization was accelerated in the negative direction (Figure 4A–B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) due to altered period responses of SCN core neurons (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: BU inhibition of NKCC1 slowed network recovery in L20 SCN slices.
source: In contrast, BU inhibition of NKCC1 slowed network recovery (Figure 4A–B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) by affecting the period of both SCN shell and core neurons (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CLP290 attenuated network recovery in L20 slices.
source: Consistent with predictions, CLP290 attenuated network recovery in L20 slices (Figure 4A–B) due to abrogation of coupling responses in both SCN core and shell neurons (Figure 4C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Bumetanide slowed the recovery of circadian waveform after release from L20 into DD in vivo.
source: Consistent with results obtained in vitro, BU slowed the recovery of circadian waveform after release from L20 into DD in vivo (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). L20 mice treated with BU displayed slower recovery of circadian waveform over time in DD due to decreased rate of activity decompression (Repeated Measures ANOVA: Drug*Time p<0.05), but BU did not significantly alter behavior after release from L12 (Repeated Measures ANOVA: Drug*Time p>0.5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: BU did not alter wheel running rhythms under entrained conditions.
source: Further, BU did not alter wheel running rhythms under entrained conditions, (Figure 5B, Repeated Measures ANOVA: p>0.5), SCN organization, body weight, water intake, activity levels, free-running period, phase angle of entrainment, or behavioral adjustment to simulated jetlag (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACE increased L12 SCN period in a GABAA-dependent manner.
source: Similar to VU, BU, and CLP290, ACE increased L12 SCN period in a GABAA-dependent manner (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACE eliminated the period difference between SCN core and shell neurons in L12 SCN slices by specifically increasing the period of SCN shell neurons.
source: ACE also eliminated the period difference between SCN core and shell neurons in L12 SCN slices by specifically increasing the period of SCN shell neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), consistent with low KCC2/NKCC1 expression in this region (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACE treatment locked the SCN network in the reorganized L20 state.
source: Remarkably, ACE treatment locked the SCN network in the reorganized L20 state (Figure 6A–B) by specifically blocking the period response of SCN core neurons (Figure 6C–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Photoperiodic changes in GABAA signaling are necessary for the functional restoration of the SCN network.
source: Collectively, these data reveal that the photoperiodic switch in GABAA signaling is necessary for the functional restoration of the SCN network and that responses of SCN core neurons are those most influenced by the photoperiodic changes in GABAA signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Seasonal changes in GABAA signaling in the SCN network regulate the transition back to its synchronous state.
source: Here we find that seasonal changes in GABAA signaling in the SCN network regulate the transition back to its synchronous state.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Seasonal plasticity in GABAA signaling may be viewed as a homeostatic mechanism because it acts to restore circuit function after it is perturbed by light.
source: In this manner, seasonal plasticity in GABAA signaling may be viewed as a homeostatic mechanism because it acts to restore circuit function after it is perturbed by light.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings presented in the discussion.

claim: Non-canonical GABAA signaling acts to impose phase differences during steady state by modulating the period of SCN shell neurons.
source: This indicates that non-canonical GABAA signaling acts to impose phase differences during steady state by modulating the period of SCN shell neurons, but facilitates synchrony in the polarized state by acting on SCN core neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Non-canonical GABAA signaling facilitates synchrony in the polarized state by acting on SCN core neurons.
source: This indicates that non-canonical GABAA signaling acts to impose phase differences during steady state by modulating the period of SCN shell neurons, but facilitates synchrony in the polarized state by acting on SCN core neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Long days decrease KCC2 in the SCN core and increase NKCC1 in the SCN shell.
source: Here we show that long days decrease KCC2 in the SCN core and increase NKCC1 in the SCN shell, consistent with previous work demonstrating that long days increase depolarizing responses to GABA in both SCN compartments (Farajnia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: KCC2 downregulation in the SCN core is the critical cellular adaptation driving network recovery in the master clock.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that KCC2 downregulation in the SCN core is the critical cellular adaptation driving network recovery in the master clock.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Slower recovery of behavioral state following systemic bumetanide administration in vivo is similar to the reduced rate of SCN recovery in vitro.
source: Slower recovery of behavioral state following systemic bumetanide administration in vivo is similar to the reduced rate of SCN recovery in vitro.
evidence: This is a comparison of findings from in vivo and in vitro experiments.

claim: Hypothalamic levels of bumetanide in the current study approached the half-maximal inhibitory concentration for NKCC1.
source: Hypothalamic levels of bumetanide in the current study approached the half-maximal inhibitory concentration for NKCC1 (Russell, 2000; Löscher et al., 2013; Hampel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the bumetanide concentration measurements with citations to support the interpretation.

claim: NKCC1 and KCC2/NKCC1 are regulated over the day under a standard lighting condition.
source: In agreement with previous work suggesting daily SCN changes in GABAA signaling correspond with altered NKCC1 expression (Belenky et al., 2010; Choi et al., 2008), our results demonstrate that NKCC1 and KCC2/NKCC1 are regulated over the day under a standard lighting condition.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to prior work.

claim: The adult SCN is likely a network in which neuroplasticity of GABAA signaling influences circuit function on both a seasonal and circadian basis.
source: Thus, the adult SCN is likely a network in which neuroplasticity of GABAA signaling influences circuit function on both a seasonal and circadian basis (Albers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citation to support the claim.

claim: Daily variation in chloride co-transporter expression may contribute to documented regional differences in neuronal excitability and GABAA responses of SCN neurons.
source: Thus, daily variation in chloride co-transporter expression may contribute to documented regional differences in neuronal excitability and GABAA responses of SCN neurons (Albers et al., 2017; Albus et al., 2005; Klett and Allen, 2017; Choi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citations to support the claim.

claim: The waveform of GABA-induced resetting displayed by L12 SCN slices replicates that elicited in previous work.
source: Consistent with this idea, the waveform of GABA-induced resetting displayed by L12 SCN slices replicates that elicited in previous work (Liu and Reppert, 2000).
evidence: This is a comparison of current findings to prior work with citation.

claim: Individual differences in SCN GABA circuits may contribute to natural variation in seasonal responsiveness.
source: Here we demonstrate that GABAA signaling regulates seasonal plasticity in the state of the SCN network, raising the possibility that individual differences in SCN GABA circuits may contribute to natural variation in seasonal responsiveness.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: GABA concentration was stable in culture for at least 24 hr.
source: GABA was not washed out following application to provide a tonic stimulus, and its concentration was stable in culture for at least 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SCN clock shifted to a later phase when GABA was applied to L12 slices at the trough of the PER2::LUC rhythm.
source: As in previous work (Evans et al., 2013), the SCN clock shifted to a later phase when GABA was applied to L12 slices at the trough of the PER2::LUC rhythm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: In L12 slices, GABA shifted the PER2::LUC rhythm in a phase-dependent manner, eliciting phase delays during early subjective night and phase advances during other times of the circadian cycle.
source: In L12 slices, GABA shifted the PER2::LUC rhythm in a phase-dependent manner, eliciting phase delays during early subjective night and phase advances during other times of the circadian cycle (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: The shape of the GABA phase-resetting rhythm in L12 slices was similar to that reported previously for GABA-induced phase shifts of electrical rhythms in dissociated SCN neurons.
source: Notably, the shape of this phase-resetting rhythm was similar to that reported previously for GABA-induced phase shifts of electrical rhythms in dissociated SCN neurons (Liu and Reppert, 2000).
evidence: This is a comparison of current findings to prior work with citation.

claim: KCC2 immunoreactivity was largely confined to the plasma membrane.
source: Importantly, cellular patterns of KCC2 and NKCC1 immunoreactivity were consistent with previous studies (Kaila et al., 2014), with KCC2 immunoreactivity largely confined to the plasma membrane and NKCC1 immunoreactivity evident in both membrane and cytoplasm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: NKCC1 immunoreactivity was evident in both membrane and cytoplasm.
source: Importantly, cellular patterns of KCC2 and NKCC1 immunoreactivity were consistent with previous studies (Kaila et al., 2014), with KCC2 immunoreactivity largely confined to the plasma membrane and NKCC1 immunoreactivity evident in both membrane and cytoplasm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: NKCC1 expression fluctuated over the day in both SCN compartments under L12.
source: In contrast, NKCC1 expression fluctuated over the day in both SCN compartments (Figure 2D, Circwave cosinor rhythmicity test: p<0.005 for each region), which is associated with daily KCC2/NKCC1 fluctuations in the SCN core (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Small changes in chloride co-transporter expression can alter the electrochemical gradient of chloride.
source: Given that small changes in chloride co-transporter expression can alter the electrochemical gradient of chloride (Rivera et al., 2002; Woodin et al., 2003), these collective changes would be predicted to increase the probability of depolarizing responses to GABA in each SCN compartment.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: VU or BU increased the period of both SCN shell and core neurons in L12 slices.
source: At the cellular level, VU or BU increased the period of both SCN shell and core neurons in L12 slices (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but did not markedly alter SCN organization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or damping of cellular rhythms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The magnitude and direction of the cellular responses depended on the core-shell relationship at the start of the recording.
source: As predicted for a coupled oscillator system (Hansel et al., 1995), the magnitude and direction of the cellular responses depended on the core-shell relationship at the start of the recording (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and citation to theoretical work.

claim: The coupling response is driven largely by changes in the cellular rhythms of SCN core neurons.
source: Analysis of cellular period indicated that this coupling response is driven largely by changes in the cellular rhythms of SCN core neurons, which adopted a longer period when the network re-synchronized in the negative direction (Figure 3C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and a shorter period when re-synchronization occurred in the opposite direction (Figure 3C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Period modulation in SCN shell neurons was less affected by phase relationship.
source: Period modulation in SCN shell neurons was less affected by phase relationship (Figure 3C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this specific neuronal subpopulation did not shift much under vehicle conditions.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: BU blocked the period responses of SCN core neurons markedly when the network was reorganized by L20.
source: Interestingly, BU blocked the period responses of SCN core neurons markedly when the network was reorganized by L20 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with the decreased KCC2 in this region under this photoperiod (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2D.

claim: Photoperiodic changes in KCC2/NKCC1 activity determine the rate and dynamics of network recovery by modulating GABAA signaling in the SCN core.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that photoperiodic changes in KCC2/NKCC1 activity determine the rate and dynamics of network recovery by modulating GABAA signaling in the SCN core.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: CLP290 increased the period of L12 SCN slices by lengthening period in both shell and core neurons.
source: Similar to VU and BU, CLP290 increased the period of L12 SCN slices by lengthening period in both shell and core neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but did not markedly alter network organization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or cellular damping over time in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effects of CLP290 in L20 slices were qualitatively similar to those induced by BU.
source: Overall, the effects of CLP290 in L20 slices were qualitatively similar to those induced by BU (Figure 4E), providing complementary evidence that the photoperiodic decrease in KCC2-mediated chloride transport is a critical modulator of intercellular coupling during network recovery from the long day state.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental findings shown in Figure 4E.

claim: After administration in drinking water, BU concentration reached 5 μM in plasma and 40 nM in the hypothalamus.
source: After administration in drinking water, BU concentration reached 5 μM in plasma and 40 nM in the hypothalamus, the latter of which approaches the half-maximal inhibitory concentration of BU for NKCC1 (Russell, 2000).
evidence: This is a finding from the bumetanide concentration measurements with citation to support the interpretation.

claim: Exposure to long days alters circadian waveform in nocturnal rodents by compressing the duration of the active phase.
source: Specifically, exposure to long days alters circadian waveform in nocturnal rodents by compressing the duration of the active phase, which is confirmed by decompression after release into DD.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about photoperiodic effects on circadian behavior.

claim: The waveform of daily rhythms is closely associated with changes in SCN state.
source: Importantly, the waveform of daily rhythms is closely associated with changes in SCN state, and decompression of the active phase manifests as the SCN returns to its synchronous state (Evans et al., 2013; Margraf et al., 1991; Jagota et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Long days shorten free-running period, but this aftereffect persists after SCN organization has recovered in vivo.
source: Long days also shorten free-running period, but this aftereffect persists after SCN organization has recovered in vivo (Evans et al., 2013; Myung et al., 2015; Pittendrigh and Daan, 1976b).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: BU did not alter water intake, body weight, activity levels, phase angle of entrainment, free-running period, or the number of days to re-entrain activity onset to a 6 hr advance of the light:dark cycle.
source: Further, BU did not alter wheel running rhythms under entrained conditions, (Figure 5B, Repeated Measures ANOVA: p>0.5), SCN organization, body weight, water intake, activity levels, free-running period, phase angle of entrainment, or behavioral adjustment to simulated jetlag (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Photoperiodic changes in the relative role of NKCC1 regulate the rate at which behavior recovers from exposure to long days.
source: This pattern of results suggests that photoperiodic changes in the relative role of NKCC1 regulate the rate at which behavior recovers from exposure to long days.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings with bumetanide.

claim: Downregulation of KCC2 alters the sign of GABAA signaling in other regions of the adult brain.
source: Because downregulation of KCC2 alters the sign of GABAA signaling in other regions of the adult brain (Hewitt et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2011; Ostroumov et al., 2016; Sarkar et al., 2011), we hypothesized that non-canonical GABA responses (i.e., depolarization) modulate the dynamics of SCN coupling after exposure to long days.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Depolarizing responses to GABA are driven by anionic gradient shifts in the flux of both chloride and bicarbonate.
source: Depolarizing responses to GABA are driven by anionic gradient shifts in the flux of both chloride and bicarbonate (Staley et al., 1995; Rivera et al., 2005), and bicarbonate regeneration is necessary for excitatory GABAA responses (Ostroumov et al., 2016; Staley et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Bicarbonate regeneration is necessary for excitatory GABAA responses.
source: Depolarizing responses to GABA are driven by anionic gradient shifts in the flux of both chloride and bicarbonate (Staley et al., 1995; Rivera et al., 2005), and bicarbonate regeneration is necessary for excitatory GABAA responses (Ostroumov et al., 2016; Staley et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Excitatory GABAA signaling in SCN shell neurons imposes the shell-core phase difference.
source: This suggests that excitatory GABAA signaling in SCN shell neurons imposes the shell-core phase difference, consistent with previous work using the non-selective chloride transport inhibitor furosemide (Myung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citation to prior work.

claim: L20 decreased KCC2 in the SCN core during the daytime.
source: Notably, long days decreased KCC2 in the SCN core during the daytime, which matches the phase when SCN neuronal responses to GABA are affected most by photoperiod (Farajnia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citation to prior work.

claim: KCC2 antagonism accelerated SCN recovery in vitro by changing the coupling responses of SCN core neurons.
source: Further, KCC2 antagonism accelerated SCN recovery in vitro by changing the coupling responses of SCN core neurons, suggesting that further suppression of KCC2 activity beyond that achieved by light may have potential benefits.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: ACE blocked network recovery by specifically modulating the coupling responses of SCN core neurons.

claim: Systemically administered bumetanide has been shown to modulate hippocampal synaptic plasticity and memory in mouse models of disease.
